Why? Over several years I came to the conclusion that there is no justice in the US and the population doesn't have an effective and realistic way to exercise authority over the government.

You can basically point to any part of American society and find something horrible wrong. People often like to call things "broken" in the US. "Our schools are broken! Our justice system is broken! Our healthcare system is broken!" but what these people don't understand is that it is their way of thinking that is "broken." The schools, justice system, and healthcare systems aren't "broken," they're operating exactly how they're supposed to: to benefit those in charge.

Here's another example: Just yesterday I was listening to a news story about how millions of US taxpayer dollars were wasted on military supplies that were supposed to be sent to Yemen, but are now rotting away in a warehouse in the US. Now, if you had the mindset that "these supplies were supposed to be sent to Yemen to try and solve a problem" you would understandably be upset at the "waste" of taxpayer money. In reality, "solving a problem in Yemen" was never the goal. Politicians made deals with weapons manufacturers to buy the supplies with US taxpayer money. The weapons dealers get paid and then turn around and support the politicians with campaign money and lucrative business opportunities. That was the point all along. There was never any real intention of solving an issue in Yemen.

This was a big realization that helped me leave. US citizens are basically tax cows. The government and private business work together to suck as much wealth and productivity out of these citizens as possible. They do this by either directly creating or encouraging the conditions necessary to create "problems" that need fixing with US taxpayer money.

ISIS/ISIL/Dash is another further good example. We needed a new "bad guy" to keep people scared and to justify spending billions on weapons. The US created the conditions needed to foster such a group so it would create the problem that it could then sell a solution to.

This is how it works. There is a lot more money to be made in treating a problem than there is in solving a problem. The US government and their business partners have no interest in solving problems, on the contrary, they want to prolong problems because that prolongs a business opportunity.

Your average tax cow, er...citizen, is taught to think about these situations as problems that need fixing. That's the whole narrative. Everyone is always talking about how to fix this problem, or fix that problem, what policy would work best, etc etc...We have news shows discussing this and political parties arguing over it. It's all theater. Left/right, conservative/liberal, it's all theater.

The world only appears "broken" if you're not the one it's built to benefit.
So what country did you move to?

Ended up moving to Berlin, Germany. When researching places to move to I made a list of things that were important to me and ranked them. No country is perfect, so my picking Germany was not some kind of endorsement of the German government. I just wanted to find a society with a different emphasis on various values and issues.

For example: Work/life balance. In the US, I had a job with 3 days vacation a year and the unspoken expectation that I was to work over 40 hours a week if I wanted to be perceived as "dedicated and hard working." Here in Berlin I have 25 days minimum paid vacation and people will give you dirty looks if you DON'T take all that vacation time. Also, you're expected to work your 40 hours and go home. If you are always working over your 40 hours people will start to wonder if there's something wrong with you.

The society here is also a lot more relaxed towards drugs, sex, and alcohol, which I find liberating. Prostitution is legal and regulated, people don't freak out at the sight of nudity, you can walk down the street with a beer in your hand and nobody looks twice, and police have better things to do than go out hunting for people smoking pot. I find the society as a whole has a lot less of a stick up its ass when it comes to social issues.

The police here are also a very different. This is an old statistic, but the trend hasn't changed much: In 2011, German police fired 85 shots. That's it. All of them. For the entire country. For the entire year. 85 shots. Of those 85 shots, 49 were warning shots. (An American cop would ask "What the hell is a warning shot?") Of the remaining 36 shots actually fired at people, 6 people were killed and 17 injured. 6 people for the entire year of 2011. The police here are fairly reserved in their use of violence compared to the US.

Berlin is also a unique city given it's history. This city was the capital of Nazi Germany. Hitler committed suicide 20 minutes from where I'm typing this. The old headquarters of the Gestapo are also nearby. After that, the city was at the center of the cold war. Check point charlie is also 20 minutes from where I'm typing this, along with the Berlin wall, the death strip, and the old Stazi headquarters. Back in the US, all that shit was just something in a movie that took place in a far away land, or a Band of Brothers special on HBO. It actually happened here. People lived it here. As such, I've found there is a greater societal sensitivity to anything that smells of fascism and an awareness of the dangers of massive state surveillance.

If you ask Berliners here on the street who Edward Snowden is, they'd most likely be able to tell you. They'd also most likely have a positive outlook of him. There's a movement here to push the government to grant him asylum and bring him to Berlin. (But that won't happen because the German government is still heavily under the influence of the US government)

Sorry if that is a long winded answer to the simple question of "where did you move to," but given that picking up everything and moving to another country is such a big and life changing decisions, I thought it deserved a little explanation.
